**Surah al-Masad (Surah 111)**
Five verses, Meccan by consensus.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Know that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. Then He explained in the surah ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1] that Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, obeyed his Lord and declared clearly the negation of worshipping partners and rivals, and that the disbeliever disobeyed his Lord and busied himself with worshipping rivals and equals. It is as if it were said: "Our God, what is the reward of the obedient, and what is the punishment of the disobedient?" So He said: the reward of the obedient is the attainment of victory, conquest and dominion in this world, and a great reward in the next, as the surah ﴿When the help of God comes﴾ indicates. As for the punishment of the disobedient, it is loss in this world and a great punishment in the next, as the surah "Perish" (Tabbat) indicates. Its parallel is His saying at the end of Surah al-An'am: ﴿And it is He who made you successors on the earth and raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ [al-An'am: 165]. It is as if it were said: "Our God, You are the Generous, free of stinginess, and the Able, free of incapacity; so what is the cause of this disparity?" He said: ﴿That He may test you in what He has given you﴾ [al-An'am: 165]. It is as if it were said: "Our God, then if the servant is sinful and disobedient, what is his condition?"

So He said in reply: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ [al-An'am: 165]. And if he is obedient and submissive, his recompense is that the Lord, exalted is He, will be forgiving of his misdeeds in this world and generous and merciful to him in the Hereafter.

They have mentioned several reasons for the revelation of this surah:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Messenger of God concealed his affair at the beginning of the mission and prayed in the ravines of Mecca for three years, until the saying of God, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214]. So he ascended al-Safa and called out, 'O Banu Ghalib!' and the Ghalib came out to him from the mosque. Abu Lahab said: 'These are the Ghalib who have come to you; what do you have?' Then he called out, 'O Banu Lu'ayy!' and those who were not of Lu'ayy came back. Abu Lahab said: 'These are Lu'ayy who have come to you; what do you have?' Then he said, 'O Banu Murrah!' and those who were not of Murrah came back. Abu Lahab said: 'These are Murrah who have come to you; what do you have?' Then he said, 'O Banu Kilab!' Then after that he said, 'O Banu Qusayy!' Abu Lahab said: 'These are Qusayy who have come to you; what do you have?' He said: 'God has commanded me to warn my nearest kindred, and you are my nearest kindred. Know that I cannot benefit you with anything of this world, nor of the Hereafter, except that you say, "There is no god but God," and I will testify to it for you before your Lord.' Abu Lahab then said: 'Perish you! Is it for this that you called us?' Then the surah was revealed."

The second: "It is related that the Messenger of God, upon him be blessings and peace, ascended al-Safa one day and said: 'Good morning, O danger!' The Quraysh gathered to him and said: 'What is the matter with you?' He said: 'Tell me, if I informed you that an enemy is about to attack you in the morning or evening, would you not believe me?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.'"

[Page 153]

Abu Lahab said what he said at that point, and then the surah was revealed.

The third: "That he gathered his paternal uncles and set food before them in a dish. They belittled it and said: 'Each of us eats a whole sheep.' He said: 'Eat.' They ate until they were satisfied, and only a little of the food was diminished. Then they said: 'What do you have?' He invited them to Islam, and Abu Lahab said what he said." It is also related that "Abu Lahab said: 'What do I get if I embrace Islam?' He said: 'What the Muslims get.' He said: 'Shall I not be given precedence over them?' The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'With what would you be given precedence?' He said: 'Perish this religion, in which I and others are equal.'"

The fourth: Whenever a delegation came to the Prophet, they would ask his uncle about him and say: "You know him best." He would tell them: "He is a sorcerer," and they would turn away from him and not meet him. A delegation came to him and he said to them the same thing. They said: "We will not leave until we see him." He said: "We have not ceased treating him for madness. Perish him and ruin!" The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was informed of this and grieved, and the surah was revealed.

\* \*

The saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾. Know that His saying "perish" (tabbat) has several interpretations:

The first: al-tabab is ruin (al-halak). From it comes the saying "a young woman who is tabbah," meaning ruined by old age. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And the plotting of Pharaoh is nothing but in ruin﴾ [Ghafir: 37], meaning in destruction. What establishes this is that when the Bedouin had intercourse with his wife during the day in Ramadan, he said: "I am ruined and I have ruined [my family]." The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, did not reject that, which indicates that he was truthful in it. There is no doubt that action is either part of faith, or if it is part of it, it is its weakest part. So when one abandons action, ruin results. In the case of Abu Lahab, there was the abandonment of belief, speech and action, and the presence of false belief, false speech and false action. How, then, can it be conceived that the meaning of ruin would not apply? Hence He said: "perish."

The second: "Tabbat" means "lost" (khasirat). Tabab is the loss that leads to ruin. From it comes His saying: ﴿And they increased them only in perdition (tatbib)﴾, meaning in loss. The evidence is that He said in another place: "other than in loss (takhsir)."

The third: "Tabbat" means "failed" (khabat). Ibn 'Abbas said: because he used to repel people from him by saying, "He is a sorcerer," so they would turn away from him before meeting him. He was the chief of the tribe and was like a father to them, so he was not suspected. When the surah was revealed and he heard of it, he became angry and showed intense hostility, so he became suspected, and his word about the Messenger was no longer accepted. It is as if his effort failed and his aim was nullified. Perhaps the hand is mentioned because he used to strike the shoulder of the one who came to him with his hand and say: "Go away rightly guided, for he is a madman." It is customary that whoever turns a person away from a place places his hand on his shoulder and pushes him away from that place.

The fourth: From 'Ata': "Tabbat" means "overcome," because he believed that his hand was the upper one, and that he would expel him from Mecca, humiliate him and prevail over him.

The fifth: From Ibn Wathhab: "His hands became empty of all good."

If it is asked: What is the benefit of mentioning the hand?

We say: There are several answers:

The first: what is related, that he took a stone to throw at the Messenger of God. Tariq al-Muharibi said: "I saw the Messenger of God in the marketplace saying: 'O people, say: There is no god but God, and you will prosper.' A man behind him was throwing stones at him, and his heels were bleeding, [and he was saying], 'Do not obey him, for he is a liar.' I asked: 'Who is this?' They said: 'Muhammad, and his uncle Abu Lahab.'"

The second: The intended meaning of "the two hands" is the whole person, as in His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Hajj: 10]. From it comes the saying: "Your hands are tied (awkat)." And His saying: ﴿Of what Our hands have made﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71]. This interpretation is reinforced by His saying "and he perished" (wa-tabb).

The third: "Perish his hands" means his religion and his worldly life, his first and his last state; or because with one hand benefit is drawn in, and with the other harm is repelled; or because the right hand is a weapon and the other a shield.

The fourth: It is related that "when he (peace be upon him) called him in the daytime, he came. When night fell, he went to his house, following the practice of Noah, to call him at night as he had called him by day. When he entered upon him, he said: 'You have come to me making excuses.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, sat before him like one in need, and began calling him to Islam. He said: 'If shame prevents you, answer me at this time and be silent.' He said: 'I will not believe in you until this kid (jadi) believes in you.' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to the kid: 'Who am I?' It said: 'The Messenger of God,' and it loosed its tongue praising him. Envy overcame Abu Lahab, so he seized the two forelegs of the kid and tore it apart, saying: 'Perish you! Magic has affected you.' The kid said: 'Rather, perish you!' So the surah was revealed in accordance with that: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾, because he tore apart the two forelegs of the kid."

The fifth: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: It is related that Abu Lahab used to say: "Muhammad promises me things which I do not think will happen, claiming that they will be after death. He has not put anything of that into my hand." Then he would blow into his hands and say: "Perish you both! I see nothing in you." So the surah was revealed.

*(And he perished.)*

As for His saying, exalted is He: "and he perished" (wa-tabb), there are several interpretations:

The first: He expressed the first as a supplication against him, like His saying: ﴿Killed be man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17], and the second in the form of a report, meaning that it occurred and took place. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and he has indeed perished" (wa-qad tabb).

The second: Each of the two is a report, but by the first he meant the ruin of his deed, and by the second the ruin of himself. The reasoning is that a person strives only for the benefit of himself and his deed, so God, exalted is He, informed that he is deprived of both.

The third: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ means his wealth, and from it comes the expression "one who has the hand" (dhat al-yad). "And he perished" refers to himself, as one says: ﴿They have lost themselves and their families﴾ [al-Shura: 45]. This is the view of Abu Muslim.

The fourth: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ means himself; "and he perished" means his son 'Utbah, according to what is related: "That 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab went out to Syria with some people of Quraysh. When they were about to return, 'Utbah said to them: 'Convey to Muhammad from me that I have disbelieved in the star when it sets.'" It is also related that "he said that to the face of the Messenger of God and spat in his face, and he was extreme in his enmity. The Prophet said: 'O God, set upon him one of Your dogs.' Terror entered the heart of 'Utbah, and he became cautious. He travelled one night, and when it was close to dawn, his companions said to him: 'The camels have perished.' They continued with him until he dismounted, frightened, and made the camels kneel around him like a pavilion. God then set a lion upon him and cast tranquillity upon the camels. The lion began to move around until it mauled him and tore him apart."

If it is said: The revelation of this surah was before this event, and His saying "and he perished" is a report about the past, so how can it be taken as such? We say: Because it was in God's knowledge that this would happen.

The fifth: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ because he did not recognise the right of his Lord, and "and he perished" because he did not recognise the right of His Messenger.

Regarding the verse there are questions:

The first question: Why did He give him a kunya (teknonym) when, if he had no son named Lahab, it would be like a lie? Also, is not the use of a kunya a form of honour?

The answer to the first: A kunya may be a name, and this is supported by the reading of one who recited: "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab," just as one says: "Ali ibn Abu Talib" and "Mu'awiyah ibn Abu Sufyan," for these people's names are their kunyas.

As for the meaning of honour, it has been answered in several ways:

The first: Since it was a name, it went beyond conveying honour.

The second: His name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, and He turned away from it to his kunya.

The third: Since he was among the people of the Fire and his end was to a fire of flame (lahab), his condition matched his kunya, so he deserved to be mentioned by it and called Abu Lahab, as one says "Abu al-Sharr" for the wicked and "Abu al-Khayr" for the good.

The fourth: He was given this kunya because of the glow and brightness of his cheeks, so it is permissible to mention him by it in mockery and contempt.

The second question: Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, was the Prophet of mercy and great character, so how is it fitting for him to address his uncle with such harsh severity? Noah, despite being at the height of harshness towards the disbelievers, said of his disbelieving son: ﴿Indeed my son is of my family, and Your promise is true﴾. Abraham, peace be upon him, addressed his father with tenderness in his saying: "O my father, O my father," while his father addressed him with severe harshness. When [his father] said to him: ﴿Indeed I will stone you, and leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46], he said: ﴿Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 47]. As for Moses, peace be upon him, when He sent him to Pharaoh, He said to him and Aaron: ﴿Speak to him a gentle word﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], even though Pharaoh's crime was graver than the crime of Abu Lahab. Moreover, in the law of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, a father is not killed for his son by way of retaliation, nor is the punishment of stoning carried out upon him; and if his father, being a disbeliever, fights against him in war, he does not kill him but repels him from himself until someone else kills him.

The answer is in several ways:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 111, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Firstly: he used to turn people away from Muhammad (peace be upon him) by saying, "He is a madman," though people did not accuse him of this, because he was like a father to him. This became something that prevented him from conveying the message to the creation, so the Messenger confronted him with this directly, until his anger grew intense and he openly showed fierce enmity. Because of that enmity, he became a suspect in disparaging Muhammad (peace be upon him), so his words about him were no longer accepted.

Secondly: the wisdom in this is that if Muhammad had been willing to compromise with anyone in religion and be lenient with him in it, such compromise and leniency would have been with his uncle, who stood in place of his father. When no such compromise took place with him, the hopes (of others) were cut off, and everyone knew that he would not show leniency to anyone in anything related to religion at all.

Thirdly: the aspect you mentioned is contradictory, for his being an uncle would necessitate that he have great compassion toward him. When the matter was reversed and great enmity arose, he rightly deserved severe harshness.

The third question: What is the reason that He did not say, "Say: Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he," and instead said in the surah of al-Kafirun: ﴿Say, O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1]?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: because the kinship of paternal uncle requires preserving respect, therefore for this reason He did not tell him to say that, lest he be directly insulting his uncle. This differs from the other surah, for those disbelievers were not his uncles.

The second: in that surah the disbelievers reviled God, so God the Exalted said: O Muhammad, answer them: ﴿Say, O disbelievers﴾. In this surah they reviled Muhammad, so God the Exalted said: Be silent, you, for I will revile them: ﴿Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab﴾.

The third: when they insulted you, remain silent until you fall under this verse: ﴿When the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63], and when you remain silent, I will be the one who answers on your behalf. It is related that a certain man used to harm Abu Bakr, and he remained silent, so the Messenger kept repelling that reviler and rebuking him. When Abu Bakr began to answer, the Messenger fell silent. Abu Bakr said: What is the reason for that? He said: Because while you were silent, an angel was answering on your behalf; when you began to answer, the angel departed and the Satan came.

Know that this is a reminder from God the Exalted that whoever does not confront the foolish, God will be his defender, his helper, and his supporter.

The fourth question: What is the basis for the reading of Abdullah ibn Kathir al-Makki, in which he would read: (abi lahbin) with the ha' unvowelled (sakinah)?

The answer: Abu Ali said: It is likely that lahab and lahb are two dialects, like ash-sham' and ash-sham', and an-nahar and an-nahr. They agreed on the vowelling of the ha' in His saying: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿nor does it save from the blaze﴾. This indicates that the fath (vowelling with a fatha) is more preferred than the sukun. Others said: They agreed on the fath only in the second instance out of regard for the harmony of the verse-endings (fawasil).

[Page 156]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What his wealth availed him, nor what he earned﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: The "mā" in His saying ﴿What availed him﴾ may be an interrogative in the sense of denial, and it may be a negation. On the first reading, the meaning is: What effect did his wealth and earnings have in averting calamity from him? No one had more wealth than Qarun, yet did he avert death from himself? No one had greater dominion than Sulayman, yet did he avert death from himself? 

On the second reading, that is a report that wealth and earnings do not benefit him in this respect.

The second issue: "mā kasaba" is in the nominative case, and "mā" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-source particle, meaning "what he acquired" or "his acquisition." It is reported that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and children." So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then they mentioned several meanings:

The first: His wealth did not benefit him, nor what he earned through his wealth, meaning the capital and the profits.

The second: The wealth is the livestock, and what he earned from their offspring and their young, for he was the owner of camels and their progeny.

The third: "His wealth" is what he inherited from his father, and what he acquired by himself.

The fourth: Ibn Abbas said: "What he earned" is his child. The evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed, the best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings." He, peace be upon him, also said: "You and your wealth belong to your father." It is narrated that the sons of Abu Lahab brought their dispute to him and fought, so he got up to separate them, and one of them pushed him and he fell. He became angry and said: "Remove from me this wicked earning."

The fifth: al-Dahhak said: "What his wealth and his wicked deeds benefited him," meaning his scheming in enmity toward the Messenger of God.

The sixth: Qatadah said: "What he earned" means his deed which he thought was of some worth, like His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].

There are questions concerning the verse:

The first question: He said here ﴿What his wealth availed him, nor what he earned﴾, and in the surah ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1], He said ﴿Nor will his wealth avail him when he falls﴾ [al-Layl: 11]. What is the difference? The answer: Expressing with the past tense is more emphatic, like His saying: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28], and His saying: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

The second question: In what did his wealth and his earnings fail to avail him? The answer: Some said, in his enmity toward the Messenger, so it did not prevail over him. Others said: Rather, they did not avail him in averting the Fire, and for this reason He said: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾.

**His saying (may He be exalted):** ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾. On this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** When God, exalted is He, informed of Abu Lahab's state in the past, saying that he was in ruin and that his wealth and his earnings did not avail him, He then informed of his state in the future, saying: ﴿He will burn in a Fire﴾.

**The second issue:** The word (sayaṣlā) ("he will burn") is read with a fatḥah on the yā' and also with a ḍammah, both lightened and doubled.

**The third issue:** These verses contain information about the unseen (al-ghayb) in three respects:

First: the information that he would be in ruin and loss, and so it was.

Second: the information that his wealth and his children would not benefit him, and so it was. Abu Rafi', the freedman (mawlā) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), narrated, saying: "I was a slave of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and Islam had entered our house. Al-Abbas embraced Islam, Umm al-Fadl embraced Islam, and I embraced Islam. Al-Abbas used to fear his people and conceal his Islam. Abu Lahab had stayed away from Badr, and he sent in his place al-As ibn Hisham, and no man of them stayed away without sending another man in his place. When news came of the event of the people of Badr, we felt strength within ourselves, and I was a weak man. I used to make arrows, shaping them in the chamber of Zamzam. I was sitting there, and Umm al-Fadl was sitting beside me, and we were pleased with the news that had reached us, when Abu Lahab came, dragging his feet. He sat down by the rope of the chamber, and my back was against his back. While he was sitting, the people said: 'This is Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib.' Abu Lahab said to him: 'How is the news, O son of my brother?' He said: 'We met the people and gave them our shoulders; they killed us however they wished. And by God, despite that, I looked at the people, and there came to us men in white, on piebald horses, between heaven and earth; they neither stood nor were struck.' Then he (Abu Lahab) struck me, and I was a weak man. Umm al-Fadl rose to a pole and struck him on the head and wounded him, and said: 'Do you think him weak now that his master is absent? By God, we have been believers for many days.' He had spoken truthfully in what he said. So he departed humiliated. By God, he did not live more than seven nights until God struck him with the pustule (ʿadasah), and it killed him. His two sons left him for two or three nights without burying him until he rotted in his house. The Quraysh used to fear the pustule and its contagion as people fear the plague, and they said: 'We fear this sore.' Then they buried him and left him." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned﴾.

Third: the information that he is among the people of the Fire, and so it was, because he died upon disbelief.

**The fourth issue:** The people of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah) argued for the occurrence of taklīf mā lā yuṭāq (imposing what cannot be borne) by saying that God, exalted is He, imposed on Abu Lahab faith (al-īmān). Among the components of faith is affirming God in everything He has informed of. Among what He informed of is that he would not believe and that he is among the people of the Fire. So he became obligated to believe that he would not believe, and this is an obligation to combine two contradictories, which is impossible. Al-Ka'bi and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri answered that if Abu Lahab had believed, this report would have had a report that he believed, not that he did not believe. The Qadi answered this, saying: "Whenever it is said: 'What if God did what He informed that He would not do, how would it be?'"

Our answer: it is not valid to respond to this with "no" or "yes."

Know that these two answers are extremely weak.

As for the first: this verse indicates that God's report of his non-faith is actual, and a true report of his non-faith is incompatible with the existence of faith, an incompatibility that is essential and cannot be removed. So if He imposed on him to come with faith while this report exists, then He imposed on him a combination of two mutually exclusive things.

As for the second answer, it is weaker than the first, because we are not seeking that they state with their tongues "no" or "yes." Rather, the plain intellect testifies that between the report of non-faith being true and the existence of faith there is an essential incompatibility. So imposing the attainment of one of two opposites while the other is present is an imposition of combining two opposites. This difficulty remains whether the opponent speaks something with his tongue or remains silent.

[Page 158]

As for His saying, ﴿and his wife, the carrier of firewood﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** It is read as *Mumayyatuhu* (with the diminutive form). It is also read *hammalata al-hatab* in the accusative, as a form of vituperation (*shatm*). The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "I prefer this reading, and it was the means by which one who loved to revile Umm Jamil approached the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." It is also read with the accusative and tanwin, and with the nominative.

[Page 158 continues]

**The second issue:** Umm Jamil bint Harb was the sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and the paternal aunt of Mu'awiyah. She was in the utmost enmity toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The scholars mentioned several explanations of why she is described as "the carrier of firewood":

The first: She would carry a bundle of thorns and thistles and scatter them at night on the path of the Messenger of God. If it is asked, "She was from a house of honour, so how can she be called a carrier of firewood?" we answer: Perhaps, despite her abundant wealth, she was base; or perhaps, because of the intensity of her enmity, she would herself carry the thorns and firewood in order to throw them on the path of the Messenger of God.

The second: She used to walk about spreading gossip. The one who goes about with tale-bearing and who stirs corruption among people is said to "carry firewood between them," meaning he kindles strife among them. And the one who talks excessively is called "a night firewood-gatherer."

The third: The statement of Qatadah, that she used to taunt the Messenger of God for his poverty, so she was taunted in return by being described as one who gathers firewood.

The fourth: The statement of Abu Muslim and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that what is meant is the sins she carried in her enmity toward the Messenger, because she is like firewood in bringing her to the Fire. A parallel to this is that God likened the doer of sin to one who walks with a load on his back. He said: ﴿They have borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾ [al-Ahzab: 58], and He said: ﴿They bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], and He said: ﴿and man bore it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72].

**The third issue:** As for *imra'atuhu* if you read it in the nominative, there are two possibilities:

The first: It is a conjunction with the pronoun in *sayaslā* (he will burn), meaning: he will burn, he and his wife. And *fi jidīhā* (around her neck) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

The second: It is nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and *fi jidīhā* is the predicate (*khabar*).

**The fourth issue:** It is reported from Asma': "When (*Tabbat*) was revealed, Umm Jamil came with a wail, and in her hand was a stone. She entered the mosque while the Messenger of God was sitting with Abu Bakr. She was saying:

*Mudhammaman qalaynā, wa dīnahu abaynā, wa ḥukmahu 'aṣaynā.*

[We have despised Mudhammam, we have rejected his religion, and we have disobeyed his command.]

Abu Bakr said, 'O Messenger of God, she has come toward you, and I fear that she will see you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'She will not see me.' And he recited: ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾ [al-Isra': 45]. She said to Abu Bakr: 'I have been told that your companion has satirized me.' Abu Bakr said: 'No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirized you.' So she turned away, saying:

*Qad 'alimat Quraysh annī bintu sayyidihā.*

[Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of its chief.]"

There are discussions regarding this narrative:

**The first:** How was it possible that Umm Jamil did not see the Messenger, while she saw Abu Bakr, when the place was the same? The answer: According to our companions (the Ash'ari scholars), the question disappears, because when the conditions are present, perception is permissible but not obligatory. If God creates perception, she sees; otherwise she does not. As for the Mu'tazilah (who hold that God is bound to ensure rational human perception under the right conditions), they gave several explanations:

The first: Perhaps he (peace be upon him) turned his face away from her and presented his back to her. Then, because of the extremity of her anger, she did not search carefully; or because God cast fear into her heart, and this fear diverted her from looking.

The second: Perhaps God cast the likeness of another person onto the Messenger, as He did with Jesus.

The third: Perhaps God diverted the ray of her sight away from that direction, so that she did not see him at all.

Know that the difficulty applies to all three explanations, because through these explanations we learn that a thing may be present and yet not be seen. And if we permit this, why should it not be permissible that there are elephants and trumpets near us which we neither see nor hear?

[Page 159]

**The second discussion:** Abu Bakr swore that he had not satirized her, and this is from the category of *ma'arid* (allusive or equivocal speech), because the Qur'an is not called satire (*hajw*), and because it is the speech of God, not the speech of the Messenger. Thus this narrative indicates the permissibility of *ma'arid*.

Two questions remain among the issues of this verse:

**The first question:** Why did He not suffice with saying "and his wife," but instead described her as "the carrier of firewood"?

The answer: It has been said that he had two other wives, so God wanted that no one should think that He meant every woman who was his wife. Rather, the intended one is only this single woman.

**The second question:** Mentioning women does not befit people of generosity and honour, so how does it befit the speech of God to mention her, especially as the wife of an uncle?

The answer: Since it was not considered improbable in the case of the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot because of the unbelief of those two women, then it is all the more fitting that it not be considered improbable in the case of a disbelieving woman whose husband is a disbelieving man.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 111, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Around her neck is a rope of palm fiber﴾. Al-Wahidi said: al-masad in the speech of the Arabs means twisting (al-fatl). It is said: masada al-habl yamsuduhu masdan, if he perfected its twisting, and a man is mamsud if he is of twisted (well-knit) build. Al-masad is that which has been twisted (masad, i.e. futila), of whatever kind it may be. So it is said of what is twisted from camel hides, and from palm fiber and palm leaves, that it is masad; and of what is twisted from iron too it is said to be masad. Having known this, we say: the exegetes have mentioned several interpretations.

The first: "Around her neck is a rope" of what has been twisted from ropes, because she used to carry that bundle of thorns and tie it around her neck, as woodcutters do. The purpose is to show her baseness, likening her to the woodcutters' women, as a way of harming her and her husband.

The second: the meaning is that her condition in the Fire of Hell will be in the form she had when she used to carry the bundle of thorns, so there will always be upon her back a bundle of firewood from the tree of zaqqum, and around her neck a rope of the chains of the Fire.

If it is said: how can a rope made of palm fiber remain forever in the Fire? We say: just as the skin, flesh and bone remain forever in the Fire. Some of them said: that masad will be of iron. And the assumption of one who supposes that masad cannot be of iron is an error, because masad is that which is twisted, whether it is of iron or of something else. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
